title: Cap. 4 Mem. 1 Rat. 1–2: Bare intrinsic sufficiency cannot ground ‘died sufficiently for all’
pass_a_gloss: Mem.1 prop: Mere sufficiency of death from intrinsic lutron-value alone, without ordinata from offerer’s mind+act, does NOT make true ‘Christ died sufficienter for all.’ Aimed at those who hold elect-only death yet admit sufficienter-for-all & exalt that sufficiency. Veteravitii at Dort: ‘for all’ can mean merit’s sufficientia/price magnitude — unique perfect lytron for all world’s sins; for reprobates twin ends (per se: God not delight in perdition, Jn 3:16; per accidens: inexcusable). Davenant: cannot rightly conceive this from nuda rei sufficientia without ordinata from offerer’s act. Proof: ‘died sufficienter for all’ = offered sufficienter / given as lytron sufficienter for all. Dying/offering/giving self for all denotes act terminated under some ordination to free all. Bare lytron-sufficiency without mind+act terminated to persons cannot make the assertion true. Common sense refuses ‘sufficienter dead for all’ of one denied dead/offered for some. Intrinsic sufficiency for 1000 worlds can coexist with lytron not yet offered for many. Debtors analogy: 10k pounds enough for five 200-pound debts, but if paid nominatim for two only, not ‘sufficiently paid for’ the three excluded — so Christ’s blood plusquam sufficiens still not sufficiently offered for those discretely excluded in the offering act. Transferring ‘sufficienter’ from dying mind/act to bare intrinsic value = playing with the received dictum. Clear sense: died for all & sufficiently, though what he sufficiently offered is not efficaciously applied to all because of intervening unbelief. Scholastic distinction sufficienter/efficaciter marks what in mode of oblation was common to elect & non-elect vs peculiar to elect. If sufficienter = bare rei value excluding ordination from offerer’s mind/act, how refer it promiscuously? If no intention except for predestinate alone, why need efficaciter limb? Bimembris distinction frivolous unless both members presupposed. Fathers urging universal sufficiency cling not to bare rei but to act/mind/mode of offering: Athanasius De incarnatione (sacrificed for all; offered for all); Augustine (blood poured for remission of all sins — mode/act, not mere intrinsic value). Scripture: 1 Tim 2:6 gave himself redemption-price for all — not ‘lytron in itself sufficient but given for few’; Jn 3:16 Father sending. Conclusion: bare sufficiency insufficient without ordinata from offerer’s mind+act toward all.
pass_b_english: 1. The mere sufficiency of Christ’s death, which is estimated from the intrinsic value alone of this lutron, without that ordained sufficiency which arises from the mind and act of offering, does not avail so far that Christ may truly be said to have died sufficiently for all. I thought this thesis should be added because of those who hold tightly that Christ died for the elect alone, and yet (I confess I am too slow to understand how) admit that Christ died sufficiently for all; and sometimes exalt this thing, a sufficiency spreading itself to all human beings, in very strong words. For they confess that Christ died for all human beings, for all orders, states, and kinds of human beings, indeed even for individual human beings as to the sufficiency of merits. The Contra-Remonstrants in the Judgment exhibited to the Synod of Dort write thus: When Christ is said to have died for all, this can be understood of the sufficiency of the merit, or the magnitude of the price. For the death of the Son of God is the one perfect and sufficient lytron for expiating and blotting out all the sins of the whole world: an immense merit of righteousness, a catholic medicine of death, a perennial fountain of life, etc. A little later: This sufficiency of the lytron, as to the reprobate, has a twin end, one of itself, the other by accident. The end of itself, that God may make it plain he does not delight in the destruction of human beings, inasmuch as he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life ([[John 3:16 >> Bible:John 3:16]]). The end by accident, that by this sufficiency of the lytron they may be rendered inexcusable. For these perish not by Christ’s fault but by their own, when by their unbelief they repudiate the benefits offered by Christ in the Gospel. So far they. This sufficiency of Christ’s death for reconciling all, I deny can be rightly conceived from a bare sufficiency of the thing offered, unless an ordained sufficiency from the offerer’s act accompanies it. Which can be proved thus.

When we say that Christ died sufficiently for all, we say nothing else than that he was offered sufficiently for all, or that he gave himself as a lytron or price of redemption sufficiently for all. But to die for all, or to be offered for all, or to give oneself for all, designates the act of one dying or offering himself, terminated under some ordination to freeing all. Therefore the mere sufficiency of the lytron, without the mind and act of the offerer terminated to persons, cannot make true this assertion, Christ died sufficiently for all. For common sense refuses that one should be granted to have died sufficiently for all who is denied to have died or been offered for some. And while the intrinsic sufficiency of the lytron for redeeming a thousand worlds stands and is conceded, it can at the same time stand that this same lytron has not yet been offered in any way for many human beings, much less sufficiently offered. For just as for freeing five debtors who each owe two hundred pounds, ten thousand pounds are more than enough; yet if this whole sum is offered and paid to the creditor by name for two only, the other three excluded, the sufficiency and superabundance in itself of this lytron will not make it that it was sufficiently given and paid for those three: so in this common cause of the human race, although Christ’s precious blood is a lytron more than sufficient for canceling the debts of all and each, yet it would not thence be affirmed to have been sufficiently offered for those who are discretely excluded in the very act of offering. They seem therefore not so much to interpret as to mock this most received and most true pronouncement of the Theologians, Christ died sufficiently for all, who transfer this term sufficiently from the mind and act of the one dying to a bare sufficiency or intrinsic value of the death considered in itself; as if the sense were, Christ’s death in itself has sufficient merit and value for blotting out the sins of all human beings, but Christ was not offered or dead for all — when the clear sense of this saying is that Christ died for all, and died sufficiently for all, although what he sufficiently offered for all is not efficaciously applied to all because of the intervening obstacle of unbelief.

In this distinction of the Scholastics, which our men commonly admit — namely that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the predestinate efficaciously — those words sufficiently and efficaciously denote what in the very mode of oblation was common to all human beings, elect and non-elect alike, and what was peculiar to the elect alone. Common to both was that Christ was sufficiently dead or offered for them as a victim to God the Father. But how will this former term, sufficiently, be referred promiscuously to elect and non-elect, if it designates a bare sufficiency of the thing, excluding the ordination of the same thing to persons that arises from the offerer’s mind and act? Or what need is there of that latter term, efficaciously, to constitute a distinction in the mode of oblation or in the offerer’s intention as to elect and non-elect, if there was absolutely no intention of Christ offering himself except for the predestinate alone? A bimembral distinction is frivolous and plainly inept where both members are not presupposed in the thing distinguished. It is to be observed, then, that the holy Fathers, urging the universal sufficiency of Christ’s death, do not stick in a bare sufficiency of the thing, but in the act, mind, and very mode of offering. So repeatedly Athanasius in the treatise On the Incarnation of the Word. I will set down one golden place: Christ the Son of God, having borrowed a body like ours, because we all were liable to death, sacrificed to his Father that same body given over to death for all. Likewise: After the monuments of his Divinity had been displayed, it remained that he should offer a sacrifice for all, delivering his temple to death for all, that he might make all free from the old transgression, etc. You see that the note of universality is joined not with the intrinsic sufficiency of the thing offered, but with the mind and act of the offerer, which looked to all. So Augustine: Christ’s blood was so poured out for the remission of all sins that it could blot out even the very sin by which it was poured. He does not say that in the blood poured out there is a sufficient intrinsic value for expiating all human beings’ sins, which is confessed among all who know how to estimate God’s blood rightly; but he urges the mode and act of offering, and in that constitutes this universality: It was so poured for the remission of all sins. It is one thing to say that Christ’s blood has from itself and in itself a sufficient value for blotting out all human beings’ sins; another to affirm that it was poured by the very fact for the remission of all sins, which Augustine said. But why do I recall the holy Fathers? Holy Scripture so speaks of Christ’s death that it does not refer its universal force to the bare dignity of the victim offered, but to the act and mind of the offerer ([[1 Timothy 2:6 >> Bible:1 Timothy 2:6]]): He gave himself a price of redemption for all. The Apostle does not say, This lytron in itself and in its intrinsic value is sufficient for redeeming all, but was in truth given for a few, not for all; but, He gave himself for all. The mind and act, then, of Christ giving himself embraced all. So also of the Father sending the Son; So God loved the world, etc. ([[John 3:16 >> Bible:John 3:16]]). That bare sufficiency of the thing, then, does not avail so far that Christ may be affirmed to have died sufficiently for all, without a sufficiency ordained toward all from the offerer’s mind and act.
source_text:
1. Mera sufficientia mortis Christi, quae ex solo valore intrinseco hujus lutri aestimatur, absque illa ordinata sufficientia quae ex animo et actu offerendi oritur, non eo valet ut Christus vere dicatur pro omnibus mortuus sufficienter. Hanc thesin apponendam putavi propter eos qui arcte tenent Christum pro solis electis mortuum fuisse, et tamen (quod ego fateor me tardiorem esse quam ut intelligam) admittunt Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter; atque hanc rem, sufficientiam ad omnes homines sese diffundentem, verbis aliquando valde exitollunt. Fatentur siquidem Christum pro omnibus hominibus, pro omnibus hominum ordinibus, statibus, generibus, imo etiam pro singulis hominibus quoad sufficientiam meritorum mortuum fuisse. Veteravitii in Judicio Dordracenae Synodo exhibito sic scribunt, Quando Christus dicitur pro omnibus mortuus, hoc intelligi potest de meriti sufficientia, seu pretii magnitudine. Mors quippe Filii Dei est unicum perfectum et sufficiens lytron expiandis et delendis omnibus totius mundi peccatis: meritum immensum justitiae, medicina catholica mortis, fons perennis vitae, etc. Paulo post, Haec sufficientia lytri, quantum ad reprobos, geminum habet finem, unum per se, alterum per accidens. Finis per se, ut Deus testatum faciat se non delectari perditione hominum, utpote qui Filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Finis per accidens ut hac sufficientia lytri reddantur inexcusabiles. Hi enim non Christi sed sua culpa pereunt, quando per infidelitatem suam beneficia a Christo in Evangelio oblata repudiant. Hactenus illi. Hanc sufficientiam mortis Christi pro omnibus reconciliandis, nego recte concipi posse ex nuda sufficientia rei oblatae, nisi accedat ordinata sufficientia ex actu offerentis: Quod sic probari potest.

Quando dicimus Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter, nihil aliud dicimus, quam pro omnibus fuisse oblatum sufficienter, vel pro omnibus dedisse se lytron sive redemtionis pretium sufficienter. Mori autem pro omnibus, vel offerri pro omnibus, vel dare semetipsum pro omnibus, designat actum morientis vel semetipsum offerentis ad omnes liberandos sub aliqua ordinatione terminatum. Ergo sola sufficientia lytri, absque animo et actu offerentis ad personas terminato, non potest veram reddere hanc assertionem, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter. Sensus etenim communis respuit, ut pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus concedatur, qui pro aliquibus mortuus sive oblatus negatur. Stante autem et concessa intrinseca lytri sufficientia ad mille mundos redimendos, simul stare potest hoc idem lytron nondum esse pro multis hominibus ullatenus oblatum, nedum sufficienter oblatum. Nam sicuti ad liberandum quinque debitores qui singuli debent ducentas libras decem mille librarum satis superque sufficiunt; si tamen haec summa integra offeratur et persolvatur creditori nominatim pro duobus solummodo, reliquis tribus exclusis, sufficientia et superabundantia in se hujus lytri non efficiet ut pro illis tribus sufficienter datum et persolutum dicatur: sic in hac communi causa humani generis, licet pretiosus Christi sanguis sit lytron plusquam sufficiens ad omnium et singulorum debita dispungenda, tamen non inde pro illis sufficienter oblatum affirmaretur, qui in ipso actu offerentis discrete excluduntur. Non itaque tam interpretari quam ludificari videntur receptissimum hoc et verissimum Theologorum pronunciatum, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, qui terminum hunc sufficienter transferunt ab animo et actu morientis ad nudam sufficientiam sive intrinsecum valorem mortis in se consideratae; quasi sensus esset, Mors Christi in se sufficiens habet meritum et valorem ad delenda peccata omnium hominum, sed non fuit Christus pro omnibus oblatus sive mortuus: cum clarus sensus hujus dicti sit, Christum pro omnibus fuisse mortuum, et pro omnibus fuisse mortuum sufficienter, quamvis quod ille sufficienter pro omnibus obtulit propter interveniens infidelitatis obstaculum non omnibus efficaciter applicetur.

In hac distinctione Scholasticorum, quam nostri communiter admittunt, Christum scilicet pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter, pro praedestinatis efficaciter, vocabula illa sufficienter et efficaciter denotant quid in ipso modo oblationis fuit commune omnibus hominibus, tam electis quam non-electis, quid vero peculiare electis solis. Commune fuit utrisque, quod Christus pro illis fuerit sufficienter mortuus sive oblatus in hostiam Deo Patri. At quomodo prior hic terminus, sufficienter, ad electos et non-electos promiscue referetur, si nudam sufficientiam rei designet, exclusa ordinatione ejusdem rei ad personas quae oritur ex animo et actu offerentis? Aut quid opus est posteriore illo termino, efficaciter, ad constituendam distinctionem in modo oblationis sive in intentione offerentis quoad electos et non-electos, si nulla prorsus intentio fuit Christi seipsum offerentis nisi pro solis praedestinatis? Frivola et plane inepta est distinctio bimembris, ubi in re contradistincta utrumque membrum non praesupponitur. Observandum itaque est, sanctos Patres universalem mortis Christi sufficientiam urgentes, non haerere in nuda sufficientia rei, sed in actu, animo, et modo ipso offerendi. Sic passim Athanasius in tractatu De incarnatione Verbi. Apponam locum unum aureum: Christus Dei Filius, a nobis simili corpore mutuato, eo quod omnes morti obnoxii essemus, pro omnibus idipsum in mortem deditum Patri suo sacrificavit. Item: Post edita Divinitatis suae monumenta, reliquum jam erat ut pro omnibus sacrificium offerret, pro omnibus templum suum morti tradens, quo omnes liberos a veteri praevaricatione efficeret, etc. Videtis notam universalitatis non cum intrinseca sufficientia rei oblatae, sed cum animo et actu offerentis, qui ad omnes spectavit, esse conjunctam. Sic Augustinus: Christi sanguis sic in remissionem peccatorum omnium fusus est, ut ipsum etiam peccatum posset delere quo fusus est. Non dicit in sanguine effuso esse sufficientem valorem intrinsecum ad expianda omnium hominum peccata, quod in confesso est apud omnes qui sanguinem Dei rite aestimare norunt; sed modum et actum offerendi urget, in eoque hanc universalitatem constituit; Sic fusus est in remissionem peccatorum omnium. Aliud est dicere Christi sanguinem habere ex se et in se sufficientem valorem ad delenda omnium hominum peccata, aliud affirmare fusum esse ipso facto in remissionem peccatorum omnium, quod dixit Augustinus. Sed quid commemoro sanctos Patres? Sacrosancta Scriptura de Christi morte sic loquitur ut universalem ejus vim non referat ad nudam hostiae oblatae dignitatem, sed ad actum et animum offerentis, 1 Tim. ii. 6. Dedit semetipsum redemtionis pretium pro omnibus. Non dicit Apostolus, Hoc lytron in se et intrinseco suo valore sufficiens est pro omnibus redimendis, sed re vera datum est pro paucis, non pro omnibus; sed, Dedit semetipsum pro omnibus. Animus ergo et actus Christi dantis semetipsum omnes complectebatur. Sicut et Patris Filium mittentis; Sic Deus dilexit mundum, etc. Johan. iii. 16. Nuda igitur illa rei sufficientia non eo valet ut Christus pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus affirmetur, absque sufficientia ad omnes ex animo et actu offerentis ordinata.
